Ugly Food: Want not, waste not.

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Why are we wasting one-third of all our food... because it's not aesthetically pleasing? We explore how perfectly nutritious food can be given a second life and what viewers can do to curb food waste

Unique Selling Point:
14 Million South African's go hungry everyday, and Statistics by the World Wide Fund have shown that almost one-third of all food produced in South Africa - totalling 10million tons of edible food - is wasted every year. We will go out with FoodForwardSA and explore how their 4 projects are saving "UGLY" food and supplying it to those who are hungry. About them: 50% of edible agricultural production is wasted due to specification requirements, cold-chain and processing inadequacies as well as access to markets. FoodForward SA is launching Second Harvest, a programme that sources and collects surplus fruit and vegetables from commercial farmers across South Africa and redistributes this fresh produce to the 600 beneficiary organisations in their network. Established in 2009 to address widespread hunger in South Africa, FoodForward SA connects a world of excess to a world of need by recovering surplus food from the consumer goods supply chain. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EwaxmKIIU2g The organisation reaches up to 250 000 daily at the cost of R0.79 per meal. Beneficiary organisations include orphanages, places of safety, creche’s, disability care, aged care, skills and youth development. The Second Harvest allows farmers to donate their post-harvest surpluses while they are harvesting, to ensure the food does not go to waste. FoodForward SA is working with a network of farmers located in the Western Cape, Gauteng, and Durban to improve the nutrition level of the groceries provided to beneficiaries. According to Managing Director of FoodForward SA, Mr Andy Du Plessis, “Dedicated refrigerated vehicles go directly to our farmers to collect fresh fruit and vegetables while they are harvesting. This fresh produce meaningfully increases the nutritional value of the food distributed, as well as volume, which significantly increases the number of people FoodForward SA are able to reach.”
Foodbanking is the most effective solution at present to reducing hunger, and reducing food waste is the third most effective solution in fighting climate change. An independent study by WWF and Green House reflects that recovering food saved 17,400 tons of green house gas emissions, which is equivalent to 3,600 cars driven every day for a whole year.
The launch of Second Harvest will ensure that more agricultural production is redistributed to the hungry. FoodForward SA encourages farmers, growers, food processors, and other supply chain stakeholders to partner with them and join the food recovery revolution.

We will have chef Jenny Morris cook with "Ugly food" and "Left overs" and potentially do a blog.


Summary:
Climate conference: Ban-ki Moon -panel commission on adaptation - to help especially poor and vulnerable countries - food security - climate. (Bangladesh). Every year in the US, 20-40% (that’s at least 1 in 5) of fresh produce is discarded even before it gets into stores because it is ‘ugly’. Like a misshapen tomato, a too curved cucumber or a lumpy potato. The ‘Ugly Fruit & Veg Campaign‘ encourages us to buy ugly and focuses not on what is on the outside, but what is on the inside – the taste and nutritional goodness of fruits and vegetables that are not visually perfect.
It is not just that there are ridiculous marketing standards that specify sizes, diameter, consistency and colour of produce (interestingly, standards don’t specify ripeness or taste); we are also the problem. We’ve been trained to shop with our eyes and to go for perfect apples, tomatoes and carrots – those that are ideally shaped, coloured and blemish-free.
Pressure from shoppers, supermarkets and farmers sees rules being shed in the US and Europe and more ugly produce is being sold alongside aesthetically appealing versions.
In the US and Europe, there are now grocery stores and home delivery services that sell ugly produce that is perfectly good to eat – and cheaper. These are ideal outlets for farmers to sell produce that is less visually appealing at a good price. Once fruit and veg are chopped up and tossed into a salad, baking dish, juice, stew or soup, does it really matter that it was misshapen when you bought it? Another bonus – children are delighted by the strange forms of wonky carrots and other misshapen veg. Buying ugly is a win-win.




Further information:
French supermarket Intermarché lauched a campaign in March 2014 and began selling scarred, disfigured, or otherwise odd-shaped fruits and vegetables at 30% less – and they sold out in their first two days. Their sexy marketing campaign pulled shoppers in, and they stayed. Here’s an English version of Intermarché’s video: According to the world resources institute: https://www.wri.org/publication/reducing-food-loss-and-waste - Essentially, one out of every four food calories intended for people is not ultimately consumed by them.
Statistics by the World Wide Fund have shown that almost one-third of all food produced in South Africa - totalling 10million tons of edible food - is wasted every year. The picture across the world is dire. Estimates are that food wasted in developing countries amounts to 1.3billion tons.

According to slowfood.com, “volunteers, chefs, farmers,producers and visitors joined forces to collect leftover food and cook together. They made, in total, more than 40000 meals out of food that would otherwise have been thrown away”.

Studio H:
I’ve highlighted a few projects below were our focus was on food waste.
- Salad 2.0 (3D printing ugly fruit & veg) http://chipsonline.co.za/3d-printing-future-fruit-salad/
- Food Studio https://www.studio-h.co.za/2017/10/03/food-studio-conference/
- Menu Design with ugly fruit & veg https://www.studio-h.co.za/2017/06/20/ads24-breakfast/
- Expo Installation to address food waste https://www.studio-h.co.za/2016/09/15/food-waste-installation/

Studio H also launched Hanna Farm Jars, a small batch preserves and pickles range using unsold produce from a local farmers market and Carrot loops using rescued carrots from grocery stores.

The picture across the world is dire. Estimates are that food wasted in developing countries amounts to 1.3billion tons.

According to slowfood.com, “volunteers, chefs, farmers,producers and visitors joined forces to collect leftover food and cook together. They made, in total, more than 40000 meals out of food that would otherwise have been thrown away”.

HOW YOU CAN DO YOUR BIT
Most food loss in South Africa happens before a meal even reaches your plate. But as a consumer, there are things you can do to help reduce your waste:
1. Plan your shopping: before hitting the grocery store, check how much of each ingredient you’ll need. Can you cook a meal with the ingredients already in your cupboards? Don’t buy more than you need to make your meal.
2. Size down your portions: pile less on your plate. The uneaten food will simply be thrown away. Rather, opt to go back for a second helping if you’re still hungry.
3. Embrace leftovers: store them, freeze them, and enjoy them at a later date.
4. Buy locally: if you buy from a local grower, you’re immediately cutting out most of the distribution chain, where much of the food waste in South Africa occurs.
5. Eat in season: out-of-season treats have to be packaged and stored. Instead, choose the foods that are abundant right now.

oRGANIC MARKET: We would meet with local entrepreneur who goes out and picks up organic food - just show what food naturally looks like - he's a great case study of how far some who are educated about nutrition are willing to go.

And then we will go to Agri Parks and the department of agriculture.http://www.gauteng.gov.za/Document%20Library/Agriculture%20and%20Rural%20Development/Service%20-Agriparks%20brochure%202016%20Webview.pdf

Press Release:


Ugly Food: Want not…Waste not
Meet a new generation of food activists, working to get food to the hungry, before it is wasted. Statistics South Africa's General Household Survey shows over 12 million people report inadequate food access. Meanwhile roughly half of all edible agricultural production is lost due to specification requirements, cold chain and processing inadequacies, plus the market tends to discard food that is not aesthetically pleasing. Carte Blanche meets celebrity chef Jenny Morris to discover how to give ugly food, that is still perfectly nutritious, a second chance – and curb waste.
Producer: Sasha Schwendenwein
Presenter: Claire Mawisa
Watch the trailer


Script:


JUST BECAUSE IT DOESN’T LOOK PERFECT, DOESN’T MEAN THAT THIS LITTLE GREEN PEPPER IS NOT NUTRITIOUS AND DELICIOUS, BUT IN SA A THIRD OF ALL PRODUCE THAT IS CONSIDERED UGLY FOOD IS THROWN AWAY.
This is because consumers won’t buy these misshapen fruits and vegetables and they therefore end up in landfills. That’s why FoodForwardSA a non profit organization decided to rescue the “Ugly food” says Andy du Plessis, it’s managing director. This process is called “food banking.”
Andy: “Food is surplus in a number of facets in our production phase, so some in our harvesting phase, some during the processing phase, and also at distribution where they store the food.”
AROUND 10 MILLION TONNES OF PERFECTLY EDIBLE FOOD IS WASTED EVERY YEAR, THAT’S ALMOST HALF OF OUR EDIBLE AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTIONS AND IT’S LOST IN SPECIFICATION REQUIREMENTS, COLD CHAIN INADEQUACIES AND ACCESS TO MARKETS.
Claire: “Are you saying that good edible food with all the nutritional value, ends up being in a landfill because it doesn’t look right?
Andy: “It looks a bit blemished there but you can use the rest of this green pepper, and its fine, and it will taste exactly the same as a shelf green pepper, in a retail store, only they discard that.”
Starting in 2009, FoodForwardSA has now spread throughout the country and their 600 food donors feed a quarter of a million people.
Andy: “All the food and non-food groceries that you see here is free.”
THE WORLD WILDLIFE FUND ARGUES THAT FRAMING EDIBLE FOOD WASTE AS SURPLUS FOOD REPOSITIONS THE DISCUSSION AROUND THE POTENTIAL OF THIS FOOD – AS FOOD AS HUMAN CONSUMPTION – TO FEED THOSE WHO ARE HUNGRY, RATHER THAN JUST WASTED FOOD, ONLY GOOD FOR COMPOST OR LANDFILLS
Pakama Community Health Centre in Gugulethu uses what would have been wasted to feed hundreds of children and elderly says Mabato Tileing.
Gogo: “They depend on this plate of food they eat, they eat at at 1, go to sleep hungry, then the next they eat at 1 again. Some of them are on medication, they can’t take it without food.”
EVEN THOUGH WE ARE LEADING ON THE CONTINENT WITH REGARDS TO FOOD BANKING, SOUTH AFRICA IS STILL VERY FAR BEHIND AMERICA AND EUROPE, WHERE FOOD BANKING IS ACTUALLY INCENTIVIZED BY GOV, THE BIGGEST ISSUE WE HAVE HERE IS THAT BIG CORPORATIONS HERE, SEE IT AS A POTENTIAL LIABILITY IF SOMEBODY GETS SICK FROM THEIR PRODUCT.
Andy: “It costs the economy roughly 60 billion rand in that loss, it’s not only the food, it’s the input costs and the resources that made that food.”
Claire: “How much does that one plate of food cost on average?”
Andy: “We have a theoretical calculation of what you call a cost per meal, and that cost per meal in the last financial year was just 79 cents.”
OFTEN IT’S IN THE LABELING THAT LEADS TO FOOD WASTE, WHEN SOMETHING IS SAID TO BE PAST ITS BEST BEFORE OR SELL-BY-DATE IT DOESN’T NECESSARILY MEAN THAT IS NOT GOOD TO EAT.
Celebrity Chef Jenny Morris joined FoodForwardSA as their ambassador to teach creative cooking with food waste. Her chicken salad uses Ugly fruit and vegetables with seasonal nectarines and reclaimed Kiwi fruit and feta cheese.
C: What do you mean by reclaimed?
Jenny: Well it’s stuff that was in the supermarket, that was edible, normally get dumped wasted, and will make some hungry person, that would be you, very happy.”
Jenny says USE your eyes, nose and taste buds they’ll tell you if something is off.
Jenny: “Spec for me is the size, shape and colour, but the flavor and the taste are amazing! And the nutritional value is there, It’s fresh produce!”
Taking UGLY food even further are food designers Sasha-Leigh Briel and Jade Ruÿzenaars from Studio H.
Leigh: “We always look at the food system, issues we’re experiencing – water crises and now food waste, and look to create a solution or create awareness by starting conversation. So then we created Hanna farm jars – we took the ugly fruit and veg that ppl didn’t want and create a range of preserves.”
They use UGLY food as their medium to run through this 3D printer… 5:00
Jade: “We cooked it down to a puree flavoured it with some spices, I we created some designs on the computer, then we created the dish - salad 2.0.”
THIS IS WHAT HAPPENS WHEN UGLY FOOD HAS BEEN MADE BEAUTIFUL AGAIN, UGLY TOMATO, UGLY CARROT AND UGLY BEETROOT HAVE BEEN RE-IMAGINED, IS THIS WHAT MODERN FOOD COULD LOOK LIKE?
Jade: “For the future you can customize your foods – add nutrition supplements also add that to your cartridges from your computer, so you can imagine you can download your meal, completely customized to your nutritional needs.”
46% OF THE WORLD’S WASTE IS ORGANIC MATERIAL, THIS INCLUDES FOOD WASTE, WHICH LEADS TO THE PRODUCTION OF HARMFUL GASSES LIKE METHANE GAS AND CARBON DIOXIDE, WHICH BOTH HAVE A SERIOUS IMPACT ON THE ENVIRONMENT SO IT FOLLOWS, IF WE REDUCE FOOD WASTE, THE HARMFUL GASSES, AND THEREFORE PROTECT THE ENVIRONMENT.
In Gauteng the Department of Agriculture and Rural Development is pioneering zero waste precision farming in their Vertical Garden on the city outskirts in Westonaria.
Makaepea: “It’s compact, you utilise the space going up - the equivalent of almost 16 tunnels of production.”
Chief Director of Agro-processing Motlatjo Makaepea says it’s about maximize space and minimizing waste.
Gdard: “As a department we are working on agro-processing program in order to try and ensure that most of the food that is produced is not wasted, but processed and preserved for later use.”
But Matome Ramalatso known as “Bones” has perfected Organic farming even within city limits. He sources toxin-free produce to sell at an Organic Market.
Bones: “Organic means food that is grown without fertilizers, pesticides, fungicides any chemical.”
He says organic farming has almost Zero waste.
Bones: “Organic agriculture can be sold to a different segment of the same market, so at the organic market you have your pretty uniformed type same size…and then within the same group you have your more natural, don’t mind if it’s three headed, it can be dirty a bit.”
Government is drafting legislation to indemnify potential surplus food donors from legal ramifications for passing on wasted food. Hopefully this will lead to surplus food going where it’s most needed. 7:15

Andy: “It costs the economy roughly 60 billion rand in that loss, it’s not only the food, it’s the input costs and the resources that made that food.” Claire: “How much does that one plate of food cost on average?” Andy: “We have a theoretical calculation of what you call a cost per meal, and that cost per meal in the last financial year was just 79 cents.” OFTEN IT’S IN THE LABELING THAT LEADS TO FOOD WASTE, WHEN SOMETHING IS SAID TO BE PAST ITS BEST BEFORE OR SELL-BY-DATE IT DOESN’T NECESSARILY MEAN THAT IS NOT GOOD TO EAT. Celebrity Chef Jenny Morris joined FoodForwardSA as their ambassador to teach creative cooking with food waste. Her chicken salad uses Ugly fruit and vegetables with seasonal nectarines and reclaimed Kiwi fruit and feta cheese. C: What do you mean by reclaimed? Jenny: Well it’s stuff that was in the supermarket, that was edible, normally get dumped wasted, and will make some hungry person, that would be you, very happy.” Jenny says USE your eyes, nose and taste buds they’ll tell you if something is off. Jenny: “Spec for me is the size, shape and colour, but the flavor and the taste are amazing! And the nutritional value is there, It’s fresh produce!” Taking UGLY food even further are food designers Sasha-Leigh Briel and Jade Ruÿzenaars from Studio H. Leigh: “We always look at the food system, issues we’re experiencing – water crises and now food waste, and look to create a solution or create awareness by starting conversation. So then we created Hanna farm jars – we took the ugly fruit and veg that ppl didn’t want and create a range of preserves.” They use UGLY food as their medium to run through this 3D printer… 5:00 Jade: “We cooked it down to a puree flavoured it with some spices, I we created some designs on the computer, then we created the dish - salad 2.0.” THIS IS WHAT HAPPENS WHEN UGLY FOOD HAS BEEN MADE BEAUTIFUL AGAIN, UGLY TOMATO, UGLY CARROT AND UGLY BEETROOT HAVE BEEN RE-IMAGINED, IS THIS WHAT MODERN FOOD COULD LOOK LIKE? Jade: “For the future you can customize your foods – add nutrition supplements also add that to your cartridges from your computer, so you can imagine you can download your meal, completely customized to your nutritional needs.” 46% OF THE WORLD’S WASTE IS ORGANIC MATERIAL, THIS INCLUDES FOOD WASTE, WHICH LEADS TO THE PRODUCTION OF HARMFUL GASSES LIKE METHANE GAS AND CARBON DIOXIDE, WHICH BOTH HAVE A SERIOUS IMPACT ON THE ENVIRONMENT SO IT FOLLOWS, IF WE REDUCE FOOD WASTE, THE HARMFUL GASSES, AND THEREFORE PROTECT THE ENVIRONMENT. In Gauteng the Department of Agriculture and Rural Development is pioneering zero waste precision farming in their Vertical Garden on the city outskirts in Westonaria. Makaepea: “It’s compact, you utilise the space going up - the equivalent of almost 16 tunnels of production.” Chief Director of Agro-processing Motlatjo Makaepea says it’s about maximize space and minimizing waste. Gdard: “As a department we are working on agro-processing program in order to try and ensure that most of the food that is produced is not wasted, but processed and preserved for later use.” But Matome Ramalatso known as “Bones” has perfected Organic farming even within city limits. He sources toxin-free produce to sell at an Organic Market. Bones: “Organic means food that is grown without fertilizers, pesticides, fungicides any chemical.” He says organic farming has almost Zero waste. Bones: “Organic agriculture can be sold to a different segment of the same market, so at the organic market you have your pretty uniformed type same size…and then within the same group you have your more natural, don’t mind if it’s three headed, it can be dirty a bit.” Government is drafting legislation to indemnify potential surplus food donors from legal ramifications for passing on wasted food. Hopefully this will lead to surplus food going where it’s most needed. 7:15

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Why are we wasting one-third of all our food... because it's not aesthetically pleasing? We explore how perfectly nutritious food can be given a second life and what viewers can do to curb food waste
metadata.Unique Selling Point: 14 Million South African's go hungry everyday, and Statistics by the World Wide Fund have shown that almost one-third of all food produced in South Africa - totalling 10million tons of edible food - is wasted every year. We will go out with FoodForwardSA and explore how their 4 projects are saving "UGLY" food and supplying it to those who are hungry. About them: 50% of edible agricultural production is wasted due to specification requirements, cold-chain and processing inadequacies as well as access to markets. FoodForward SA is launching Second Harvest, a programme that sources and collects surplus fruit and vegetables from commercial farmers across South Africa and redistributes this fresh produce to the 600 beneficiary organisations in their network. Established in 2009 to address widespread hunger in South Africa, FoodForward SA connects a world of excess to a world of need by recovering surplus food from the consumer goods supply chain. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EwaxmKIIU2g The organisation reaches up to 250 000 daily at the cost of R0.79 per meal. Beneficiary organisations include orphanages, places of safety, creche’s, disability care, aged care, skills and youth development. The Second Harvest allows farmers to donate their post-harvest surpluses while they are harvesting, to ensure the food does not go to waste. FoodForward SA is working with a network of farmers located in the Western Cape, Gauteng, and Durban to improve the nutrition level of the groceries provided to beneficiaries. According to Managing Director of FoodForward SA, Mr Andy Du Plessis, “Dedicated refrigerated vehicles go directly to our farmers to collect fresh fruit and vegetables while they are harvesting. This fresh produce meaningfully increases the nutritional value of the food distributed, as well as volume, which significantly increases the number of people FoodForward SA are able to reach.” Foodbanking is the most effective solution at present to reducing hunger, and reducing food waste is the third most effective solution in fighting climate change. An independent study by WWF and Green House reflects that recovering food saved 17,400 tons of green house gas emissions, which is equivalent to 3,600 cars driven every day for a whole year. The launch of Second Harvest will ensure that more agricultural production is redistributed to the hungry. FoodForward SA encourages farmers, growers, food processors, and other supply chain stakeholders to partner with them and join the food recovery revolution. We will have chef Jenny Morris cook with "Ugly food" and "Left overs" and potentially do a blog.

Every year in the US, 20-40% (that’s at least 1 in 5) of fresh produce is discarded even before it gets into stores because it is ‘ugly’. Like a misshapen tomato, a too curved cucumber or a lumpy potato. The ‘Ugly Fruit & Veg Campaign‘ encourages us to buy ugly and focuses not on what is on the outside, but what is on the inside – the taste and nutritional goodness of fruits and vegetables that are not visually perfect. It is not just that there are ridiculous marketing standards that specify sizes, diameter, consistency and colour of produce (interestingly, standards don’t specify ripeness or taste); we are also the problem. We’ve been trained to shop with our eyes and to go for perfect apples, tomatoes and carrots – those that are ideally shaped, coloured and blemish-free. Pressure from shoppers, supermarkets and farmers sees rules being shed in the US and Europe and more ugly produce is being sold alongside aesthetically appealing versions. In the US and Europe, there are now grocery stores and home delivery services that sell ugly produce that is perfectly good to eat – and cheaper. These are ideal outlets for farmers to sell produce that is less visually appealing at a good price. Once fruit and veg are chopped up and tossed into a salad, baking dish, juice, stew or soup, does it really matter that it was misshapen when you bought it? Another bonus – children are delighted by the strange forms of wonky carrots and other misshapen veg. Buying ugly is a win-win.

They made, in total, more than 40000 meals out of food that would otherwise have been thrown away”. HOW YOU CAN DO YOUR BIT Most food loss in South Africa happens before a meal even reaches your plate. But as a consumer, there are things you can do to help reduce your waste: 1. Plan your shopping: before hitting the grocery store, check how much of each ingredient you’ll need. Can you cook a meal with the ingredients already in your cupboards? Don’t buy more than you need to make your meal. 2. Size down your portions: pile less on your plate. The uneaten food will simply be thrown away. Rather, opt to go back for a second helping if you’re still hungry. 3. Embrace leftovers: store them, freeze them, and enjoy them at a later date. 4. Buy locally: if you buy from a local grower, you’re immediately cutting out most of the distribution chain, where much of the food waste in South Africa occurs. 5. Eat in season: out-of-season treats have to be packaged and stored. Instead, choose the foods that are abundant right now. oRGANIC MARKET: We would meet with local entrepreneur who goes out and picks up organic food - just show what food naturally looks like - he's a great case study of how far some who are educated about nutrition are willing to go.
